summary: R. Yitzchak Nappacha objects that vestment removal may be a prohibition, not a positive commandment; the verse's placement in the service sequence resolves it as a required act. The Gemara then debates whether slaughtered blood retains its legal identity as 'blood of a bull' (Abaye: yes; Rava: disputed). The central dispute: Abaye holds the HP's bull is a communal sin-offering overriding Shabbat/tumah; Rava holds it is personal.

learning.ahaMoment: The same verse can yield a positive commandment or a prohibition depending on whether it is read as prescribing an act or banning continued conduct.
learning.memoryAnchor: Removing linen vestments - is it an obligatory ceremony at service end or only a ban on wearing them afterward?
learning.learnerQuestion: Is 'he shall remove his linen garments' a positive commandment requiring active removal, or only a prohibition against continuing to wear them after service?
learning.coreTension: The verse can be read as creating either a positive commandment to actively remove the vestments at a specific time, or merely a prohibition against wearing them outside their permitted context, and each reading has different legal consequences.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara debates whether 'he shall remove his linen garments' is a positive commandment with independent legal force or only a prohibition, with R. Yitzchak Nappacha establishing it as a genuine positive commandment requiring an affirmative act of removal.

takeaway.text: The verse 'he shall remove his linen garments' generates a positive commandment to actively remove the vestments, not merely a prohibition against continued wearing - it imposes a required action, not just a restriction.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may read the vestment-removal verse as purely prohibitory - don't continue wearing them - missing that R. Yitzchak Nappacha establishes it as a positive commandment requiring an affirmative act of removal.

learning.ahaMoment: Slaughter changes the animal's existence but may not change the blood's legal identity - the label depends on legal convention, not biological fact.
learning.memoryAnchor: After slaughter: is it still 'bull blood' or just 'blood'? The Abaye-Rava dispute turns on whether legal categories follow biological states.
learning.learnerQuestion: After the High Priest's bull is slaughtered, does its blood legally remain 'the blood of a bull' for Yom Kippur purposes, or does slaughter change its legal identity?
learning.coreTension: Abaye holds that slaughtered blood retains its category as 'blood of a bull,' preserving the legal identity needed for the Yom Kippur service, while Rava disputes this, creating uncertainty about whether the blood has the required legal status once the animal is dead.
learning.coreMove: Abaye and Rava dispute whether slaughter changes the legal identity of the blood: Abaye maintains it retains its offering-category status as 'blood of a bull,' while Rava holds that slaughter does change the blood's legal characterization, leaving the service's legal grounding open to challenge.

takeaway.text: Whether slaughtered blood retains its legal identity as 'blood of a bull' is disputed: Abaye holds it does, preserving the offering's legal character; Rava disputes this, holding slaughter changes the blood's legal characterization.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume that because the blood came from the bull, it automatically and permanently retains its legal identity as 'bull's blood,' missing that Rava specifically challenges this assumption.

learning.ahaMoment: The HP brings the bull 'for himself' yet represents all Israel - the tension between these roles drives the communal/personal classification dispute.
learning.memoryAnchor: HP's bull: 'for himself and his household' - personal (Rava) or communal representative (Abaye)?
learning.learnerQuestion: Is the High Priest's Yom Kippur bull a communal offering brought on behalf of all Israel, or a personal offering for himself and his household?
learning.coreTension: Abaye, following R. Meir, holds the bull is a communal chatat because the High Priest represents all Israel; Rava holds it is personal, based on 'for himself and his household,' and the two positions rest on competing readings of the same verses and traditions.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara frames the dispute as turning on whose interests the High Priest represents when he brings the bull: Abaye with R. Meir reads the HP as a communal representative, while Rava reads 'for himself and his household' as the limiting scope, making the offering personal.

takeaway.text: Abaye with R. Meir holds the High Priest's bull is a communal sin-offering because the HP represents all Israel, while Rava holds it is personal because 'for himself and his household' limits its scope - this is an active, unresolved dispute.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume the High Priest's representative role as national leader settles the question in favor of a communal offering, missing that Rava explicitly disputes this based on a competing reading of the verse.

misconceptions.correction: The Gemara frames this as an active dispute: Rava holds the bull is personal because the verse limits its scope to 'himself and his household,' and Abaye's communal reading with R. Meir is one position in the argument, not the settled ruling.

rashiTranslations.en: He shall take out the entire bull - this apparently shows that even after slaughter it is called 'bull'; the resolution is that he shall take out
all of it - this is the resolution, meaning: it is not that the blood is called 'bull,' but rather he means: he shall take out
all that remains of it. New difficulty: 'and the bull of the sin-offering' - this is a difficulty, for it is written (Leviticus 16)
'and the bull of the sin-offering' regarding Yom Kippur, and after its blood has already been given the verse speaks
of taking them out for burning. New comment: 'in skin, flesh, and dung' -
where the verse speaks of the bull's body itself - its skin,
flesh, and dung all together - there,
everyone agrees it is called 'bull.' New comment: 'when do they disagree' -
regarding entry into the inner sanctum, where he brings in there
only the blood. New comment: 'with what was he rendered fit to enter' - what
shall he do so that he may be permitted to enter? He shall bring
a live bull into the courtyard and perform the services appropriate to the matter.
'But let him derive it' - this is the difficulty we raised above, that perforce
another bull cannot enter through its own slaughter as a substitute, for indeed
it is a sin-offering whose owners have died. New comment: 'a communal
sin-offering it is' - since it comes on behalf of himself and his fellow
priests (and on behalf of the entire congregation of Israel),
as it is written, 'and he shall atone for himself and for his household' (and for
the entire congregation of Israel) (there). New comment: 'he said to him, Rabbi
Meir' - this matter is discussed in Tractate Temurah (14a). New comment: 'does this not imply
that there is one who says it is communal' -
does this not imply that he (Rabbi Meir) heard the first Tanna say
it is communal, and that is why it overrides Shabbat and tumah. New comment: 'he said
to him, Rabbi Yaakov' - this responds to the first Tanna of Rabbi Meir's statement:
both of them are replying to a single Tanna, who said
a communal offering overrides Shabbat and tumah; an individual offering does not
override. New comment: 'the chagigah' - it will explain further on
why it is called a communal offering. New comment: 'the griddle-cakes of the
High Priest' - their time is fixed every day, like the daily-offering.
The chagigah's time is not fixed enough to override Shabbat,
since it has make-up days throughout the seven festival days. New comment: 'all of them
shall die' - since it has now become a sin-offering whose owners have otherwise achieved atonement,
and there are five sin-offerings that must die: the offspring of a sin-offering,
the substitute of a sin-offering, a sin-offering whose owners died,
one whose owners achieved atonement elsewhere, and one whose year has passed. New comment: 'for a
communal sin-offering does not die' - for was the tradition of the five
sin-offerings that die taught only regarding an individual's offering? New comment: 'to a voluntary offering' -
for the altar's constant use, and it is called a communal freewill-offering,
coming from the leftover proceeds of all the animals set out to graze
mentioned throughout. Rashi's textual note: the correct reading is 'but it was taught:
the bull of Yom Kippur and the goat of Yom Kippur' that were lost.
New comment: 'for a partnership's sin-offering does not die' - for Rabbi
Shimon holds the five sin-offerings that die
were taught by God to Moshe together in one place, so that just as
the substitute of a sin-offering that dies does not apply in partnership,
since a partnership's offering does not undergo substitution,
as it is written, 'and if he shall indeed exchange it' (Leviticus 27) - language of
an individual - so too, none of them die when owned by the community, nor
by partners, even those causes of death that apply to them, and thus
it is explained in Tractate Horayot (6a). New comment: 'and what difference does it make' -
since in any case it does not go to death, and indeed
Rav Amram's answer above resolves the difficulty we raised,
'let him derive it from the fact that it is a sin-offering whose owners died' -
why did it matter to Rava to depart from Rav
Amram's language of calling it a communal sin-offering,
and to establish it instead as a partnership's sin-offering? New comment: 'that
the priests do not bring a bull for an erroneous ruling' - meaning:
in resolving our difficulty we certainly agree it can be resolved either way, whether
it is called a communal sin-offering or called
a partnership's sin-offering - but it was not satisfactory to
Rava to call them communal, so that the students should not say
that if a court of
priests ruled to violate one of the commandments,
and the priests acted upon their ruling, one might think they would bring
a bull for an unwitting communal sin like that of one of the other tribes,
since we hold (Tractate Horayot 5b) that a single tribe is called
a 'congregation' - but the priests are certainly not called
a 'congregation'; rather, only those who took a tribal inheritance in the land are.
According to the one who says, etc. (continues on 50b).
